elements.quote: Cytokine release syndrome with elevated levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6) is associated with multiorgan damage and death in severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). As of October 2020, cumulative moderate-certainty evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) showed that the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab reduces the risk of mechanical ventilation in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, without affecting short-term mortality [1].
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the current state of knowledge about IL-6, cytokine release syndrome, and summarizes prior trial evidence about tocilizumab's effects and remaining uncertainty regarding mortality.

elements.quote: Our objective was to update the data in a living systematic review of the literature concerning the ef fi cacy and toxicity of the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab in COVID-19 patients.
elements.reason: The abstract and introduction state the objective and rationale for conducting an updated (living) systematic review to evaluate tocilizumab efficacy and safety, explaining the importance and need for the review.

elements.quote: Using the same methodology and search databases detailed in our previous review [1], we searched for new studies published through 24th February 2021 and updated our analysis using the same quality assessment tools and analytical methods.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly cites and refers to a previous review, states this is an update using the same methods, and explains the need for the current updated review.

elements.quote: Cytokine release syndrome with elevated interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels is associated with multiorgan damage and death in severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). ... the ef fi cacy and toxicity of the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab in COVID-19 patients.
elements.reason: The text describes the biological context (IL-6–mediated cytokine release) and identifies tocilizumab as an IL-6 receptor antagonist, providing the proposed mechanism of action for the intervention.

elements.quote: the ef fi cacy and toxicity of the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab in COVID-19 patients.
elements.reason: The review concerns a single pharmacologic agent (tocilizumab) rather than a complex, multi-component intervention or delivery context; no logic model is provided or relevant.

elements.quote: Objectives: Cytokine release syndrome with elevated interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels is associated with multiorgan damage and death in severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). elements.quote: The participants were hospitalized COVID-19 patients, and intervention was tocilizumab versus placebo or standard of care.

elements.quote: Eight RCTs, with 5340 patients, examined the effect of tocilizumab on short-term mortality; pooled RR was 0.91 (95%CI 0.78 e 1.07, I 2 25%). Seven RCTs, with 5391 patients, examined the effect of tocilizumab on risk of mechanical ventilation; pooled RR was 0.84 (95%CI 0.76 e 0.93), I 2 0%, ... Eight RCTs, with 5340 patients, examined the effect of tocilizumab on a composite of poor outcome; pooled RR was 0.82 (95%CI 0.76 e 0.90, I 2 3%). Data from the RCTs showed a lower risk of infections and no higher risk of serious adverse events with tocilizumab: pooled RR 0.67 (95%CI 0.45 e 0.99, eight RCTs) and 0.85 (95%CI 0.63 e 1.16, seven RCTs), respectively.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists multiple outcome domains sought (short-term mortality, mechanical ventilation, composite poor outcome, infections, serious adverse events) in the abstract.

elements.quote: Survivor bias was addressed in the analysis in 11 out of 28 studies only. The pooled RR of the 11 studies that adjusted for survivor bias was 0.48 (95%CI 0.35 e 0.67). To study the potential effect of survivor bias on the observed results, we multiplied the RR ... and pooled the new adjusted effect estimates. The corrected pooled adjusted RR for mortality from the 28 cohorts was 0.69 (95%CI 0.53 e 0.89, I 2 83%)
elements.reason: The authors describe an explicit assumption/adjustment made for missing/biased information (survivor bias): they note which studies addressed survivor bias and describe multiplying RRs and recalculating pooled estimates to correct for survivor bias, indicating assumptions/adjustments were described.

elements.quote: Using the same methodology and search databases detailed in our previous review [1], we searched for new studies published through 24th February 2021 and updated our analysis using the same quality assessment tools and analytical methods.
elements.reason: While the authors state they used 'the same quality assessment tools', they do not name or cite any specific tool or instrument used to determine which data items to collect in the provided evidence; no explicit citation or name of a tool for selecting data items is given.

No information is provided about adaptations made to an existing risk-of-bias tool.

No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment (use, training, performance, validation) are mentioned in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: We pooled crude risk ratios (RRs) of RCTs with a random effects model and evaluated inconsistency between studies with I 2 .
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the effect measure used (risk ratios / RRs) for the pooled analyses and reports RRs throughout the results and tables/forest plots.
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect sizes (e.g., definitions of small/medium/large effects) or rationale for such thresholds are reported in the provided evidence.
The manuscript does not describe any methods to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure in the provided evidence.
Although the effect measure (RR) is reported, the provided evidence does not include a justification for choosing that effect measure.

elements.quote: Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies at low or moderate risk of bias. The participants were hospitalized COVID-19 patients, and intervention was tocilizumab versus placebo or standard of care.
elements.reason: The manuscript states which study designs and participant/intervention types were eligible for inclusion, indicating some criteria used to decide which studies contributed to syntheses. However, it does not describe the detailed processes used to decide which studies were eligible for each specific synthesis (for example, tabulating intervention characteristics and comparing against planned groups or explicit rules for grouping studies into each synthesis).

elements.quote: As several RCTs have been published since our initial review, and as per peer reviewers' and editor's recommendations, this update includes observational studies up to January 2021, and future updates will include only data from RCTs. We also contacted all fi rst authors of eligible RCTs for additional data for subgroup analyses.
elements.reason: This provides additional information on decisions about which study types were included in this update and that authors sought additional data for subgroup analyses, showing some aspects of how studies were selected for particular analyses. Still, it lacks explicit stepwise processes or criteria used to decide eligibility for each separate synthesis (e.g. how trials were grouped by intervention characteristics or outcome definitions).

No text in the provided evidence explicitly describes methods used to prepare data for presentation or synthesis (e.g., handling of missing summary statistics, imputation, data conversions or transformations). The Methods and Results chunks refer to using the same methodology and analytical methods as a previous review and to contacting authors for additional data (text_6), but do not provide details about data preparation or conversions.

No methods section text describes the tabular structures used to display results or the specific data included in tables. While tables (Table 1, other result tables) are present in the Results, the manuscript does not describe in Methods how tables were constructed or what data fields they would include.

elements.quote: "Fig. 1. (A) Forest plot for the effect of tocilizumab on 28 e 30 days mortality in randomized controlled trials. (B) Forest plot for the effect of tocilizumab on risk for mechanical ventilation in randomized controlled trials. However, the Methods do not describe the graphical methods in detail (e.g., software, plotting conventions, summary statistic plotting choices), so the reporting is partial.

elements.reason: The tables and figures visibly group studies (e.g., headings in tables/figures such as '1.4.1 Double-blind RCTs' and '1.4.2 Open label RCTs' in tables/figures and subgroup labels in forest plots), showing an ordering/grouping used. However, the Methods do not state the explicit basis or rationale for this ordering/grouping (it is implicit from labels), so reporting is partial.
All visual displays shown are standard (tables and forest plots). There is no evidence of non-standard graphs being used, and therefore no rationale for non-standard graphs is applicable.
No software package name or version number is reported in the provided evidence.
No description or justification of alternative synthesis or summary methods when meta-analysis was not possible is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Only the two largest RCTs d the RECOVERY [6] and REMAP-CAP [8], in which > 80% of the patients were treated concomitantly with corticosteroids d showed an improved survival in patients receiving tocilizumab. We could not examine the interaction between corticosteroid use, mechanical ventilation, timing of tocilizumab, in fl ammatory markers, and the effect of tocilizumab on different outcomes. We contacted all authors of the eight RCTs asking them for data for different subgroups; only one author provided us with the needed data. Despite the eight published trials in the past year, it is still dif fi cult to specify which population will bene fi t from tocilizumab in COVID-19. Ambiguity is compounded when taking into consideration the differences in trial designs, such as inclusion criteria of patients with different disease severity, and the temporal trends in standard of care (such as the use of steroids) (Table 1). There are many variables that may dictate who will bene fi t from tocilizumab treatment, such as patient characteristics, disease severity, timing of treatment, and duration of illness (Table 1). Data from the RECOVERY trial showed that the survival bene fi t was restricted to patients who received concomitant steroids rather than patients who did not: RR 0.80 (0.70 � 0.90) versus 1.16 (0.91 � 1.48) respectively. We concur with the recommendations by the expert panels of the Infectious Disease Society of America [20] and National Institute of Health COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines [21] that tocilizumab should be used in combination with dexamethasone in hospitalized adults with COVID-19 who: (a) within the prior 24 e 48 hours have required high- fl ow supplemental oxygen, noninvasive or mechanical ventilation, and (b) are receiving low- fl ow oxygen and have increasing oxygen requirements and elevated in fl ammatory markers despite dexamethasone.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly compares the review findings with results from major RCTs (RECOVERY, REMAP-CAP), notes how concomitant corticosteroid use may modify effects, acknowledges differences in trial designs and populations, and cites guideline recommendations—thereby interpreting results in the context of other relevant evidence.
